captions.text: Hi Chloe.
You're in Year Five now,
getting ready for the New South Wales
selective high school test in twenty twenty seven.
Keep a pencil and some paper nearby.
Each lesson gives you a puzzle.
Pause, try your own idea, then watch how the clues fit together.
Afterwards, try a fresh question.
Come back tomorrow and see if you can explain the idea again.
Try four moves.
First, name the kind of puzzle.
Next, sketch the clues.
You might draw a line for a race or a grid for matching names.
Now decide what the clues tell you.
Finally, prove it.
Point to the clue that makes your answer work.
If you're stuck, try one of the choices against your sketch.
One small word can change the job.
If the question asks what must happen,
your answer has to work every time the rules are followed.
Could happen?
Show one way that works.
Cannot happen?
Show which rule it would break.
In a race, before allows a gap.
Immediately before means there's nobody between the two runners.
Let your drawing remember the clues for you.
For a rule, draw an arrow.
For a race, draw spaces for the runners.
To match people to pets, use a grid.
Two overlapping circles can show who joined both clubs.
When a shape turns, follow a mark near one corner.
Choose the picture that helps you answer this question.
Start with a short puzzle.
Once you can explain it, try the same idea in a longer story.
Underline what you need to find.
Sketch just the clues that matter.
Later, mix different kinds of questions and try some with a timer.
Getting a short example right is a good first step.
Your selective high school test is in twenty twenty seven,
for Year Seven entry in twenty twenty eight.
The New South Wales Department of Education lists forty multiple
choice questions in forty minutes for the Thinking Skills section.
That's about one minute per question on average.
While you're learning, pause and take the time you need.
Later, try an official practice test on a computer.
An arrow is a promise.
Start at the tail, where the rule says what has to happen.
At the tip is the result you can count on.
If the starting fact is true, the rule promises the result.
A pattern that holds only some of the time cannot make that promise.
Here comes the blue card.
The rule says the gate opens whenever that card is scanned.
We have the scan, so we can follow the arrow.
The gate must open.
Cover the first part and imagine you saw only an open gate.
Could you tell which card opened it?
Your turn.
If Chloe attends robotics, she catches the late bus.
Chloe attends robotics today.
What must she do?
Draw the arrow and give a one-sentence proof.
Pause if you want more thinking time.
Chloe catches the late bus.
The rule starts with attending robotics,
and that is exactly what Chloe did today.
You can follow the arrow forwards.
Seeing Chloe on the late
bus another day would leave open how she got there.
Necessary means required.
Sufficient means enough by itself.
A requirement is like a ticket:
without it, the result is blocked,
but having it may not be enough.
Ask whether a condition is a requirement
or a guarantee before deciding which way your arrow should point.
Every finalist handed in a form.
Here is the form Mia handed in yesterday.
Imagine the pile of forms beside the list of finalists.
Every finalist has a form in the pile.
Could Mia have a form in the pile and still miss the final?
Yes. The form was required.
Mia might still miss out.
A qualifying time is required for relay selection.
Zoe has achieved that time.
Can we prove that she will be selected?
Name what we know, and what is still uncertain.
We can prove Zoe ran the qualifying time.
Imagine two runners who both ran that time
but there is just one place left.
One might miss out.
The rule still holds.
Getting the time clears a hurdle,
but the rule never promises a place.
Start with a rule that always holds.
If the first thing happens, the second must happen too.
Now suppose the second thing is missing.
Could the first have happened?
It would have left the very sign you are missing.
That backwards check is called the contrapositive.
If a valid code card is scanned, the scanner beeps.
The scanner did not beep.
Therefore a valid code card was not scanned.
That is the whole conclusion.
It does not tell us whether an invalid card was scanned
or no card was scanned at all.
Whenever a player finishes a match with exactly three goals,
the coach writes a report.
The coach wrote no report for this player’s match.
What can you be sure of about the number of goals that player scored?
The player scored a number of goals other than three.
Exactly three would have meant a report.
Two goals still fit the clues.
Four goals also fit.
We ruled out one number without deciding
whether the player scored more or fewer than three.
A desk lamp comes on whenever you press its button.
You walk in and find the lamp on.
Did anyone press the button?
A timer might have switched it on.
And if nobody pressed the button,
the timer could still light the lamp.
One way to make something happen need not be the only way.
If the hall is booked for training, the coach opens it.
The coach opened it.
Must training be booked?
No. The coach might open it for an assembly.
The original rule still holds, but the proposed reversal fails.
One legal alternative is enough to defeat that must claim.
In this puzzle, every lemon is sour.
This fruit is not a lemon.
Must that mean it is not sour?
Think of one fruit that would break that claim
while still obeying the lemon rule.
No. Picture a green lime with sour juice.
That fruit tastes sour, and it is different from a lemon.
Our example follows the rule about lemons
and still breaks the claim about this fruit.
One way to get a sour taste does not have to be the only way.
Imagine two rules.
Win a game and you collect a badge.
Collect a badge and you get a turn on the slide.
Can you follow both rules after a win?
Yes. The first one ends with collecting a badge.
The second starts in exactly the same place.
Now try that with a different pair of rules.
If the gate is locked, visitors use the side entrance.
If visitors use the side entrance, they sign the book.
The gate is locked.
Follow the complete chain: locked gate, side entrance, signed book.
Signing is guaranteed because each step has its own stated rule.
The same two rules hold for every visitor.
A locked gate sends them to the side entrance.
Using the side entrance means signing the book.
One visitor left without signing.
Could the gate have been locked when that visitor arrived?
Work back, one link at a time.
The gate was not locked.
No signature rules out using the side entrance under these rules;
that rules out a locked gate.
We reversed and negated each link.
We did not simply reverse the original positive arrows.
Listen to this promise.
“The picnic goes ahead unless it rains.”
Take rain out of the picture.
Now the picnic must go ahead.
If rain comes, that promise no longer settles what happens.
It might still go ahead under cover.
Try the same trick with “provided that”.
“The picnic goes ahead provided it stays dry”
and “the picnic goes ahead as long
as it stays dry” both make dry weather enough.
The rule says you cannot collect equipment
unless a coach is present.
Today the coach is away.
Can you collect the equipment?
No. To collect it, you need a coach there.
Tomorrow the coach might be there,
but that alone would not promise you the equipment.
The outdoor concert proceeds unless it rains.
It does not rain.
What follows?
First say the rule using if not, then apply it to the fact.
If it does not rain, the concert proceeds.
We have no rain, so it proceeds under the stated rule.
We cannot use that sentence
alone to decide what must happen if rain does occur.
One result may have several routes.
Draw each route separately,
and do not assume the result identifies one of them.
You can eliminate routes only when
the question gives enough information.
To conclude that one listed route must occur,
the list must cover all allowed routes.
Here are the only two ways to reach the final.
A team earns at least fifteen points,
or it wins the Fair Play award.
This team is in the final with thirteen points.
Cross off the points route.
That leaves one way in.
The team must have won Fair Play.
A badge can be earned through training or through a challenge.
Sam has a badge.
Does that prove Sam completed training?
Explain the alternative that prevents a definite conclusion.
Sam could have earned the badge by completing the challenge.
That one example is enough to show why training is uncertain.
Notice the difference from our team:
there we were told the complete list and could cross one route out.
Usually, often, tends to, may,
and likely express less than certainty.
They allow exceptions.
Circle these words before you judge a conclusion.
A statement about what commonly happens cannot,
by itself, prove what must happen in one particular case.
Players who miss training are usually dropped.
Katya missed training but was not dropped.
One student claims she must have a medical exemption.
That does not follow.
The usual pattern allows exceptions,
and the rule never identifies the reason for Katya's exception.
Students who read daily tend to score well.
Leo reads daily.
Must he score well?
Explain which word limits how strong your conclusion can be.
Leo might score well.
Circle the words “tend to”.
They describe a pattern across students,
and Leo can be an exception.
Daily reading and a lower score
can both be true without breaking this statement.
When a question gives two speakers, evaluate them separately.
First translate the rule.
Then record each person's claim, whether it follows, and why.
One speaker being wrong does not make the other correct.
Only after both checks should you choose a combined answer.
Imagine two different days.
When the national team plays,
every shop in this puzzle puts up its flags.
Rob sees no flags.
The team cannot be playing there that day,
because the flags would be up.
Paul sees flags on the other day.
Could shops also put up flags for a parade?
Yes. Only Rob can be certain.
Consider two different trials.
If a robot detects red, it beeps.
Ava hears a beep in her trial and says the robot detected red.
Ben hears no beep in his trial and says it did not detect red.
Which speaker reasons correctly?
Test both claims from the same rule.
Only Ben reasons correctly.
No beep rules out a red detection under this absolute rule.
Ava reverses the arrow: another input might also cause a beep.
The explanation matters more than remembering the answer combination.
When somebody says something must happen,
they mean it happens every time the rules are followed.
Try to make their claim false.
Can you still follow every rule?
If you can, show them your example.
Even one example is enough to break that must claim.
Ava stands before Ben, and Ben before Chen.
Dani's position is unrestricted.
Chen must be after Ava because the chain forces it.
Ava need not be first: Dani,
Ava, Ben, Chen is a legal counterexample.
Both conclusions come from the same small line diagram.
Ava stands before Ben, and Ben stands before Chen.
Dani can stand anywhere.
Must Chen finish the line?
Try putting somebody behind Chen.
Does your new line still follow both rules?
Try Ava, Ben, Chen, Dani.
Ava is before Ben.
Ben is before Chen.
Both rules work, yet Chen is third.
One arrangement that fits the rules and breaks the claim is enough.
If someone says Chen must be last, you can show them this line.
Could means that at least one legal case exists.
Force the proposed answer to be true,
fill in everything else,
and check every rule.
A partial arrangement is not enough.
Once you have one complete legal case,
you have proved possibility and can stop.
The café must open on four weekdays, including Monday and Friday.
Mark Monday and Friday open first.
We need two more open days.
Can we leave Wednesday closed?
Choose Tuesday and Thursday.
Count the four open days, then check both required days.
This week works.
That single week proves Wednesday could be closed.
Four children stand in a line.
Ava must be before Ben, and Chloe is not first.
Could the order Dani, Ava, Chloe, Ben work?
Check each rule separately.
Yes. Ava is before Ben, and Chloe is third rather than first.
The complete order satisfies both rules, so it could work.
We do not need to show that every arrangement has this order.
If a proposed case is impossible,
every attempt to build it has to break a rule.
Try making the case work.
Find the rule that stops you, however you arrange the other pieces.
One failed attempt proves
little if you still have other possibilities to try.
Five spaces, exactly three cars.
Try filling every space.
By the time the fourth car arrives,
you have already broken the rule.
No arrangement of five cars can rescue the idea.
But could the first space contain a car?
Yes. Use spaces one, two and three and leave the other two empty.
A whole number is greater than forty and less than fifty.
A friend says it could be
fifty because fifty is the top number on the sign.
Is that possible?
Name the largest number that does fit.
Forty-nine is the largest number that fits.
A number has to be smaller than fifty to pass the upper limit.
It also has to be bigger than forty.
Now change the rule to say “at most fifty”.
That new wording includes the endpoint.
One small word can move the boundary.
Some means at least one.
None means zero.
If someone says “not all the singers came”,
at least one singer missed out.
Now try “every square card is blue”.
You can say what a square card would look like,
but there might be no square cards in the box.
And a blue card could be round.
Someone tells you, “Not all the choir came to rehearsal.”
Picture a roll call.
If every name had a tick, the speaker would be wrong.
So at least one tick must be missing.
Could every singer have stayed home?
Yes. One missing tick is all the words promise.
More are possible.
Some square cards are striped.
No square card is green.
What must be true about at least one striped card?
Track the cards whose existence is guaranteed by some.
At least one striped card is not green.
The striped square cards exist
because the first statement says some,
and every square card is excluded from green.
We cannot claim that all striped cards are squares
or that none are green.
To prove that an answer is undetermined,
build two legal cases that give
different answers to the exact question.
Simply saying there is not enough information is weaker.
The two cases show precisely what can change
while every stated relationship remains true.
Leo is shorter than Nina and taller than Max.
We can line up those three from tallest to shortest.
Where does Sam go?
Try putting Sam above the entire group.
Sam is tallest in that line.
Now put Sam below everyone else.
The original leader is tallest again.
Both lines fit the clues.
We cannot name one certain winner.
This bag holds only red, green and blue marbles.
There are four red and two green.
We know there is at least one blue marble,
but we do not know how many.
Which colour has the fewest?
Try changing only the blue number.
Can you make the answer change?
It is undetermined.
If there is one blue marble, blue is least common.
If there are three blue marbles, green is least common.
Both cases match the facts,
so no single least common colour is forced.
An argument asks you to accept a conclusion
because of some evidence.
Find what the author wants to prove,
then what information supports it.
Finally name the gap:
what must connect that evidence to the conclusion?
This structure guides strengthen, weaken, flaw,
and assumption questions.
A teacher compares a mathematics club with other pupils.
The club members scored higher.
The teacher decides that joining the club caused the higher scores.
Now ask who joined in the first place.
Perhaps those pupils already had higher scores before they joined.
The result alone cannot tell us which story fits.
A survey of chess club members finds
seventy per cent prefer strategy games.
A student concludes that most students
in the school prefer strategy games.
Identify the evidence, the conclusion, and the gap.
The chess club gave us the number:
seventy per cent of those surveyed prefer strategy games.
The student has changed the group to everyone in the school.
Would pupils outside the club answer the same way?
Until we know that,
the result tells us about the people who answered.
To strengthen an argument,
find evidence that makes
its conclusion more convincing by targeting the gap.
A statement can share the topic without supporting the reasoning.
Compare options by how directly they remove the main doubt,
rather than whether they sound positive.
Suppose two classes start at about the same spelling level.
One does a short vocabulary review each day.
The other carries on as usual.
Both take the same spelling test.
If the review class gains more marks,
that tackles the claim directly.
A class saying it likes the worksheets would tell us much less.
A school says its new shelter keeps uniforms drier on rainy days.
Which finding tests that claim better?
One group says it likes the paint.
Another compares uniforms
after pupils wait the same time in the same rain,
some under cover and some outside.
Which would you use, and why?
Choose the second test.
It measures the wetness of uniforms.
If the children under cover
arrive drier after the same wait in the same rain,
that supports the claim.
Liking the paint would tell us about taste.
A beautifully painted shelter could still leak.
To weaken an argument,
find something that makes its conclusion
harder to believe from the evidence given.
Maybe a second change could explain the result.
Maybe the proposed fix misses the real problem.
A fact can sound like bad news
and still tell you nothing about this particular claim.
Late homework submissions fell after a new reminder system began.
The school credits the reminders.
But teachers also started calling
parents about missed deadlines at the same time.
Those calls provide an alternative explanation,
so the fall alone cannot confidently be credited
to the reminder system.
A council expects new bike racks to increase cycling.
A survey finds that unsafe routes,
rather than missing storage,
are the main reason residents do not cycle.
Does this strengthen or weaken the proposal's reasoning?
Name the barrier.
It weakens the council’s argument.
A bike rack helps once you reach the end of the trip.
It cannot give you a safer route on the way there.
Some people might still use the racks,
but the survey gives us a reason to expect fewer
new cyclists than the council hopes.
A flaw question asks what is wrong with the reasoning step,
rather than asking for a new opposing fact.
Common errors include treating correlation as cause,
using a biased sample,
reversing a requirement,
or treating missing evidence as proof that nothing happened.
Explain the structural mistake in ordinary words.
In this competition,
every prize winner must have attended the workshop.
Noah attended, so an observer says he will win a prize.
The rule runs from prize winner to workshop attendance.
The observer reverses it, treating a requirement as a guarantee.
Attendance alone does not prove that Noah will win.
Nobody submitted a complaint about a new rule,
so the rule's supporters conclude that nobody disliked it.
What is the flaw?
Explain why the observation does not guarantee the conclusion.
Think of one pupil who dislikes the rule but keeps quiet.
Would the school receive a complaint from that pupil?
No. Now every fact in the question can stay true
while the claim “nobody disliked it” is false.
The missing step is assuming
everyone who dislikes a rule will speak up.
A necessary assumption is an unstated part the argument depends on.
Identify the gap, then negate a candidate assumption.
Ask whether the argument's support breaks.
Merely helpful information is not necessarily required.
Negate the meaning carefully: not all is not the same as none.
The council says more people will cycle
because the new bike storage solves a problem.
Whose problem?
There must be someone who holds back
because there is nowhere secure to leave a bike.
Try the opposite: nobody holds back for that reason.
The council has just lost its reason for expecting extra riders.
A school predicts that offering online parent interviews
will increase attendance by making interviews easier to access.
What assumption about at least some parents who
currently miss interviews does this explanation need?
Negate your answer to test it.
At least some parents who currently miss interviews
must find the online option easier to use.
Imagine none of them do.
Then easier access cannot explain
extra attendance among those parents.
Another change might help,
but the school would need a different explanation.
Two things occurring together do not automatically establish cause.
Check four possibilities:
the proposed direction,
the reverse direction,
a third factor affecting both,
and weak or chance evidence.
A cause claim needs more support than a correlation
or a simple before-and-after observation.
Children who read more often also know more words.
Does reading teach them words?
It could.
Now turn the arrow around.
A child who already knows many words may find reading easier
and choose more books.
The two ideas could even work together.
The survey alone cannot tell us which direction the arrow goes.
Schools with more trees have cooler playgrounds.
Which comparison better tests shade's effect:
two schools measured on different days,
or shaded and nearby unshaded areas measured
at the same time under comparable conditions?
Explain the choice.
Use the nearby shaded and unshaded spots, measured at the same time.
Now a cooler day at one school cannot explain the difference.
Try using the same surface in both spots too.
Otherwise, measuring grass in one and hot concrete
in the other could give a different answer for another reason.
For a survey, ask four questions:
who was surveyed, how many,
how they were chosen,
and who is missing.
Compare the sample with the population named in the conclusion.
A large number of responses does not automatically
remove selection bias or make a sample representative.
A survey of chess club members finds that most enjoy strategy games.
Concluding that most students in the school
enjoy them goes beyond the sample.
Chess club members are selected from a group already
likely to enjoy this kind of activity.
Other students may have different preferences.
Six hundred parents answer a voluntary
online poll about a school rule.
Does the large response count guarantee a representative sample?
Name a bias that can remain even with many responses.
Six hundred is a lot of replies.
But imagine the link mostly
caught the attention of parents who felt strongly.
Six hundred of their replies might tell a different
story from the views of all parents.
Ask who chose to reply and whose views you still have not heard.
Before you compare two results,
ask: are we using the same measuring stick?
If one road carries more traffic, check crashes per trip.
For two classes, check where their scores started.
Also check the time,
how the counts were made,
and anything else that could change the result.
Pick the check that matters for this question.
The first road had forty crashes.
The second road had twenty.
The bigger total looks worse.
Suppose the first road had four thousand trips
and the second had one thousand.
For every hundred trips,
the first road had one crash and the second had two.
Without the trip counts,
the original totals cannot settle which road is riskier.
This year's class scores higher
after a new programme than last year's class did.
Before crediting the programme,
what starting condition should we compare?
Explain why the two final scores may not be a fair test.
Compare the classes' starting ability or earlier scores.
This year's class might already have been stronger.
Without a fair starting comparison,
the difference in final scores may reflect different
students rather than the programme's effect.
Recorded counts depend on both what exists
and how easily it is detected or reported.
More sightings do not always mean more actual cases.
Ask whether both groups had the same chance of being noticed,
measured, or recorded.
A change in reporting rules can also create an apparent change.
Observers recorded one hundred and thirteen sightings of red frogs
and fifteen sightings of green frogs.
Imagine a green frog sitting against green leaves.
A visitor might walk straight past.
If red frogs stand out more,
the tally could favour red even when equal numbers live there.
We have counted sightings, not every frog.
Reported bullying falls by thirty per cent after a policy starts.
At the same time, minor incidents stop being recorded.
How does that change affect
the claim that the policy reduced actual bullying?
Identify what was measured differently.
It weakens the claim based on the recorded fall.
The measurement rule changed,
so fewer reports could occur
without an equivalent fall in actual bullying.
This does not prove the policy failed;
it shows that these counts cannot by themselves establish its effect.
Picture a finish line.
Ava crosses before Ben.
Could someone squeeze between them?
Try Ava, Sam, Ben.
The clue still works.
Now change just one word.
If Ava finishes immediately before Ben, Sam no longer fits there.
Draw an arrow for “before”.
Save a joined pair for “immediately before”.
Ava finishes before Ben, and Ben finishes before Chloe.
Join the two clues through Ben: Ava, then Ben, then Chloe.
Ava must finish before Chloe.
However, another runner could finish between Ava and Ben.
Our chain proves relative order;
it does not prove that anyone finishes first, second,
or third overall.
Liam is ahead of Noah.
Priya is between Liam and Noah.
What order is forced?
Do the clues require consecutive places?
The forced order is Liam, Priya, Noah.
Their places do not have to be consecutive.
Someone else may stand between them without breaking either clue.
We have proved order, not adjacency.
Imagine clipping two name cards together.
Mia must stand immediately before Noah.
Read from the front of the line: Mia, then Noah, with no gap.
You can move that pair along the line.
You cannot turn it round.
If the clue only said “next to”, either order would work.
Mia is immediately before Noah, and Noah is immediately before Eli.
These clues overlap at Noah,
so they form one three-person block:
Mia, Noah, Eli.
Nobody can be inserted inside it.
Other people may go before or after the block,
but the three people must stay together in this order.
Three books are red, blue, and green.
Red is immediately before blue.
Green is next to blue.
What is their order?
The books are red, blue, green.
Red already occupies the place immediately before blue,
so green must use the other neighbouring place.
The two adjacency clues now fit one block.
Imagine three chairs in a row.
Start at the first chair and walk to the third.
It takes two moves to get there.
Look back.
Only the middle chair is between your start and finish.
For places apart, count the moves.
For places between, count only the chairs inside the gap.
Five boxes stand in a row,
with positions numbered one to five from left to right.
Black is at the far right, so it occupies position five.
White is two positions to its left,
so subtract two: white is in position three.
Position four lies between them.
The remaining boxes need not be arranged.
There are five seats.
Ava sits at one end, and Ben sits immediately beside Ava.
Which position numbers could Ben occupy?
Ben can occupy position two or position four.
If Ava sits in position one, Ben is in two.
If Ava sits in five, Ben is in four.
Keep both legal cases.
Imagine looking down at a round table.
Across the table means opposite.
Clockwise means the way the hands on a clock move.
Left is different: it belongs to the person in the clue.
Turn your page until you face the way that person faces.
Now point to their left.
Draw four seats around a table.
Use north, east, south,
and west as diagram labels,
and anchor Ava at north.
Chloe is opposite Ava, so Chloe is south.
Ben is one seat clockwise from Ava, so Ben is east.
Dina takes west.
These clues describe relative seats,
so rotating the whole drawing keeps the same circular arrangement.
Ava is in the north seat, facing inward towards the table.
Ben is in the east seat.
Is Ben on Ava’s left or right?
Ben is on Ava’s left.
At the north seat, Ava faces south towards the table.
Her left hand points east.
Always establish the person’s facing
direction before interpreting left or right.
Imagine putting activity cards on a timetable.
A card that says “Tuesday morning” has one home.
Put it there.
A card that says “afternoon only” could fit any free afternoon.
Cross out mornings, then look again.
A clue that looked weak may now leave just one place.
There are three activity slots:
Monday morning, Monday afternoon,
and Tuesday morning.
One activity fills each slot.
Music is Tuesday morning, and art must be in the afternoon.
That puts art on Monday afternoon.
Chess takes the remaining slot, Monday morning.
Fixed time and availability solve the timetable without guesswork.
Training happens only in the morning,
and events only in the afternoon.
The hall opens only for these activities.
It opens this morning. Why?
It opens for training.
An afternoon-only event cannot explain a morning opening,
and the rules allow no other reason.
Eliminating the impossible
activity leaves training as the only option.
Think of a row of lockers.
We can know a locker’s owner before we know its colour.
Write the locker numbers across the page.
Put names in one row and colours in another.
A name and a colour in the same column belong to the same locker.
Leave the other boxes open until a clue fills them.
Three lockers, numbered one to three from left to right,
are blue, red, and green,
with each colour used once.
The first locker is blue.
Ari owns the third locker.
The red locker is immediately to the left of his.
That puts red in the middle.
The only colour left for the third locker is green.
Four lockers are numbered one to four from left to right.
The red locker is immediately left of Ava’s.
Which position is impossible for Ava?
Ava cannot own locker one.
There would be no locker to its left for the red locker.
We can prove this position impossible
without knowing any of the other colours or owners.
Ava, Ben and Cara are lining up.
Imagine two line-ups still fit every clue.
Another clue might be true in both.
Knowing it would leave you stuck.
Or it might fit just one.
Then you know the whole order.
Try each extra clue on the original list, and count what still fits.
There are exactly three people.
Ava is before Ben, and Cara is not first.
The possible orders are Ava, Ben, Cara and Ava, Cara, Ben.
Adding Ava is first changes nothing
because both orders already satisfy it.
Adding Cara is before Ben leaves only Ava, Cara, Ben,
so that clue is sufficient.
Two orders still fit.
In the first, Ava leads, followed by Ben, then Cara.
In the second, Ava leads, followed by Cara, then Ben.
Here is a new clue.
Ben finishes before Cara.
Does that clue settle the whole order?
Yes. Ben before Cara keeps Ava, Ben, Cara and rejects Ava, Cara, Ben.
Exactly one legal order remains,
so the new clue is sufficient for determining
the complete arrangement.

Nobody else can have the compass,
so cross out the rest of its column.
Kai, Mila, and Noah bring a camera, compass,
and torch, one different item each.
The compass belongs to neither Kai nor Mila, so Noah has it.
Kai does not have the camera.
With the compass already used, Kai must have the torch.
That leaves the camera for Mila.

Each pet has a different owner.
The three pets are a cat, a dog and a fish.

Another clue rules out a cat for Ana.
Out of Ana, Bo and Cy, who owns the dog?
The dog belongs to Ana.
The fish already has an owner.
The clues say that the cat belongs to someone else.

Now the dog and the fish are taken.
The cat must belong to Bo.

Your choices are Leo and Maya.
If you must pick at least one person,

You can also take both.

You must pick exactly one person.
Which choice breaks that rule?
Picking the pair would give you two people.
Exactly one of Leo and Maya is selected.

Leo yes and Maya no,
or Leo no and Maya yes.
Both selected breaks exactly one.
Neither selected also breaks it.

reliably than a vague feeling that someone should be picked.

Is bringing both pens allowed?
What possibility does the notice exclude?
Both pens are allowed.
The notice requires at least one of the two colours,
so it excludes bringing neither.
Red only, blue only, and both all satisfy the stated rule.

In one, Leo joins.
In the other, Maya joins.
Give each version its own row.
Add only the people its clues require.
If a name is missing from a clue, leave a question mark there.

Exactly one of Leo and Maya is selected.
Selecting Leo requires Nina; selecting Maya requires Omar.

In Maya’s case, Omar is selected.

What must happen in either case?

unless further rules exclude the other event.

Put your finger on the first clue.
Does the line-up obey it?
Move to the next clue.

Ava is before Ben, and Cara is first, not last.

Cara cannot finish last.

Ben comes first.
Cara is in the middle.
Ava comes last.

Cara is not last, but passing that rule cannot rescue the option.

You can solve it without picking someone to trust.
Pretend one runner won.
Read each statement as if that were so.
Give true statements a tick and false ones a cross.

Only one runner wins.

Ben picks Cara.

The second says blue.
The third says it is not red.
Exactly two statements are true.
Which colour fits?

The next two speakers are right.

Try a red prize or a green prize.
Each would give only one correct statement.

look for a clue such as “some members swim”.

Every dancer stays outside the group marked with the letter X.

Yes fits both codes, so you are still stuck.

For each answer you could receive,
ask yourself the same thing:
would I know what I came to find?

Yes leaves twelve and thirteen.
No leaves twenty-four and thirty-four.
Neither answer pins down the code.

Four codes cannot each get their own answer
when there are only two answers to give.
There are just two possible codes left.
One is twelve.
The other is thirteen.

Does the code end in the digit two?
Think about both possible replies.
Will the reply always tell you the whole code?

The question is decisive because it separates

Can you slide it to the finish without jumping a gap?

Add a path from park to school.
Now we can travel from library to park, then school, then pool.
A link within one original pair would not connect the two groups.

Which new link would let you travel from A to D: A–B or B–C?
Add B to C.
The route becomes A, B, C, D, with every step connected.
Adding A to B again would leave the two groups separate
and would not reach D.

Keep going the same distance on the other side.
Your pencil moves across the page, never up or down.
Now try turning the whole page upside down.
The dot would change height.

Is a half-turn an equivalent transformation?
The dot stays high

A half-turn would move it low.

from rotation without relying on the overall impression.

The whole drawing turns around that point.

like a clock hand moving from twelve to three.

You never need to flip the page over.
Start with the marked L and turn it ninety degrees
clockwise about the marked turning centre.
The marker in the upper-left
quadrant moves to the upper-right quadrant.
The long arm and foot turn together.

moving the dot alone would not be a valid rotation.

Give it a half-turn around the marked centre.
Where does the high dot on the left end up?
Could you make this turn just by turning your page flat on the table?
The dot ends up below and to the right of the centre.

the same distance from the centre.

The L turns with the dot.

Another is three cubes tall and stands behind it.

Its top sticks up by one cube.

Which floor squares have a stack on them?
The front row has heights one, two, one.
The back row has heights two, three, two.

The middle column is three high,

Should stacked cubes be counted separately?
Six squares appear in the top view.
All six ground positions are occupied,
so each contributes one square.

Stacked cubes share the same ground position.
Put a dot just beside a fold.
When you open the paper,
its partner appears the same distance across the crease.
Now put the centre exactly on the crease.
How far across is its partner?
Zero. Both centres land on one spot.

Number the columns one to four.
Name the rows A to D from the top.
Fold the right half left, then the top half down.
Punch through all the layers at the centre of square D one.
Open the top fold first.
You get D one and A one.
Open the side fold.
Their partners appear in D four and A four.

but away from the horizontal fold line.
After both folds open, how many distinct hole centres appear?
Two distinct hole centres appear.
Reflection across the vertical fold leaves the point unchanged.
Reflection across the horizontal fold creates its partner.

Two squares far apart on the page might touch as the box closes.
One thing is certain: opposite faces can never touch.
Pair up the opposites.
To make a cube corner, choose one face from each pair.
Two opposite faces in your choice rule that corner out.

Follow the strip to the right.
The far end folds over to face the middle square.

The top and bottom squares give another pair.
The squares immediately left
and right of the middle give the third pair.

After folding, could A and F share an edge?
Could A, D and E all meet at one corner?

At the visible corner,
the top flap touches the right flap and the closing flap.
Read the three labels around that corner.

Keep that face up and slide the die around without tipping it.
Its four side faces visit the front in a fixed order.
You cannot swap only two side faces and leave the others still.
The opposite pairs help you
fill in the hidden faces before you test a turn.
A standard die shows one on top, two at the front,
and three on the right.
Five is at the back because it is opposite two.
Turn the die clockwise as seen from above, keeping one on top.
Three moves from right to front, and five moves from back to right.
The displayed new view is possible.

can a rotation keep one on top
while changing to front three and right two?
No. Keeping one on top
and moving three to the front puts five on the right, not two.

A two-square piece cannot fill three empty squares.
That rules it out straight away.
If a piece has the right number, trace its outline with your finger.

If the tiles have a pattern,
check that the marks meet across the edges too.

contains an L-piece in the top-left, bottom-left,
and bottom-middle cells.
Three cells remain empty: top-middle, top-right, and bottom-right.
The missing piece must fill exactly those cells.

but it also needs the correct bent shape;

the displayed three-cell gap without overlap or gaps,
even if you rotate the strip?

The empty cells form a bent L,
while the strip stays straight under rotation.

Swap the first two cards.
The card with the letter B is now first.
The card with the letter A is in the middle.

The middle arrow stays up.
The last arrow points left.

Turn each of those arrows a quarter turn clockwise.

The last card points down.

Draw a little arrow on the dot for the way you face.

If you walk, move the dot too.

The park is east of the library.
The museum is north of the park.
Start at the library,
move east to the park,
then north to the museum.
The museum is both east and north of the library,
so it is northeast.

or require the two legs to be equal.
You are facing west.

Which compass direction do you face now?
You face north.
Follow the compass clockwise from west:
the next quarter-turn reaches north.
Your position has not changed;
only your facing direction has changed.

Make a small key as soon as you learn a pair.
In this code, each letter has its own symbol.
If two letters match, their symbols match.
If the letters differ, their symbols differ too.
Now check the positions one at a time.

The letter M means triangle.

Write the word moon and fill its four spaces.

Next come two circles, one for each middle letter.
The last space takes a square.
Use the same code.

Write all four symbols, and check which positions must match.

Square, circle, circle, square.

so each takes a square.
The two inside spaces both hold the letter O,
so each takes a circle.

R is present but is not second.

A fills the remaining box.

Skip whole groups to get near your bead.

You're on the last bead of a complete group.
The colours go red, blue, green, yellow.
Which colour is at position twenty-six?

Move one more place for red.
Move a second place for blue.
That puts blue at position twenty-six.

Red is first.

so it lands on the fourth item.

all others work.

Would zero and eight still look different?

and the defect removes its upper-left segment.

so this faulty shape alone cannot identify the original digit.
A marker can move around a board
and change its appearance at the same time.
Make a separate row for each feature.

Another might record its dots.
After the same number of moves, read the rows together.

Each move goes clockwise to the next corner and adds one dot.

After four, it returns to top left.
Count the dots now.
There are five.
The corner repeated, but the whole picture did not.
A marker first returns to its starting position after four moves,
and its colour first returns after three.
Both cycles repeat.
After how many moves do both starting states first return together?
Both return together after twelve moves.
Twelve is the smallest positive multiple of both four and three.
It completes three position cycles and four colour cycles,
so both features reset at the same time.

The last digit arrives at the front.
Each digit turns too.

turn six, one, nine upside down.

Nine comes first, then one, then six.

has one in the middle,

even though seven days have passed.

a second to Thursday,
and a third to Friday.

Counting Monday as visit one,
how many days after Monday is visit three?

Keep those units beside the numbers.

How many pencils does it use?
How many stickers?

The first supply to run short sets your limit.

We have eighteen pencils and twenty-one stickers.

Undo doubling by halving.

How much extra distance does this detour add?

At what time must they leave?

The other rewards the biggest improvement.
